introduction-the-event-you-cannot-predic.core: Black swans are rare, high-impact events that history doesn't predict (Taleb's turkey felt safest the day before Thanksgiving). You can't forecast them, but you can build systems that survive surprises.

first_principles.problem: Teams plan only for failures they've already seen, so the unprecedented one is catastrophic.
truths: Past stability doesn't guarantee future stability.
Robustness can be designed without prediction.
derivation: Design for **static stability** and **loose coupling**; **practise** failure.

analogy.title: Taleb's turkey
analogy.story: 1,000 days of being fed builds confidence, right up to the day it ends.
analogy.breaks: Over-preparing for every conceivable disaster is unaffordable, so focus on classes of failure.

example.title: A long-stable region
flow: Services that depend on it can't recover

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Uptime history isn't evidence of future safety.

example.outcome: design for surprise, not just history.

check.a: That a long history of stability can create false confidence right before a catastrophic, unforeseen event.

the-taxonomy-of-ignorance-unknown-unknow.core: Known knowns are understood and monitored, known unknowns are risks you're aware of but can't fully quantify, and unknown unknowns are failures you haven't imagined. Defences differ for each: monitoring, risk planning, and generic resilience plus exploration.

first_principles.problem: Teams focus only on known failure modes and are blindsided by novel ones.
derivation: **Unknown unknowns**: generic resilience (redundancy, isolation, degradation) + chaos experiments.

analogy.title: A map with blank regions
analogy.story: Some areas are mapped, some marked 'unexplored', and some you don't even know exist until you sail into them.
analogy.breaks: Classification isn't static: today's unknown unknown becomes tomorrow's known risk.

example.title: Classifying risks
flow: Known unknown: vendor API outage duration
Unknown unknown: surfaced by chaos test → DNS TTL issue

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: An unknown becomes known and gets fixed.

check.q: How do you defend against unknown unknowns?
check.a: With generic resilience (redundancy, isolation, graceful degradation) and experiments that uncover hidden failure modes.

the-region-wide-failure.core: Entire cloud regions do fail (us-east-1 outages have cascaded through many services). Systems should treat a region as a failure domain and be able to survive or recover from losing one.

first_principles.problem: Engineers assume a region is too big to fail and build everything in us-east-1 with no plan.
truths: Global services sometimes depend on one region.
derivation: Treat the **region as a failure domain**.
**Know the hidden dependencies** (global services anchored in one region).

analogy.title: A city-wide blackout
analogy.story: Every building's backup generator matters when the whole grid goes down, not just one building's wiring.
analogy.breaks: Multi-region is expensive and complex, so prioritise the critical paths.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Map what you'd lose if a region vanished.

check.q: Why should an entire region be considered a failure domain?
check.a: Regional outages have happened, and shared regional services can take down everything inside the region.

control-plane-vs-data-plane-outages.core: The data plane serves running traffic (existing instances, load balancers forwarding packets). The control plane creates and changes resources (APIs to launch, scale, configure). Control planes are more complex and fail more often, so the data plane should keep working without them.

first_principles.problem: During a control-plane outage, autoscaling and failover scripts that call cloud APIs fail exactly when they're needed.
truths: Control planes are complex, with many dependencies.
Data planes are simpler and highly available.
Recovery actions often need control-plane APIs.
derivation: Avoid **recovery that needs control-plane calls** (launching instances during failover).

analogy.title: An office building's operations vs. its management office
analogy.story: If the management office closes, lights and lifts keep running, but you can't book new rooms.
analogy.breaks: Some workloads must scale during events, so balance pre-provisioning cost against risk.

branches.label: Design
children: Steady state needs data plane only

example.title: A failover design flaw
flow: Failover script launches instances in region B (control plane)
Redesign: warm capacity pre-provisioned in B
example.outcome: systems that keep serving when management APIs fail.

check.q: Why shouldn't failover rely on launching new instances?
check.a: Launching uses the control plane, which may be impaired during the very outage you're recovering from.

strategy-static-stability.core: A statically stable system keeps working, with no changes needed, when a dependency fails. Capacity is pre-provisioned, configuration and credentials are cached, and decisions are pre-computed, so an outage never requires a reactive control-plane action.

first_principles.problem: Systems recover by scaling up or reconfiguring, actions that depend on the very services that are failing.
truths: Reactive recovery depends on working control planes.
Cached data keeps working when its source fails.
derivation: **Over-provision** across AZs so losing one needs no new launches.
**Cache** config, DNS and credentials with long validity.
**Fail static**: keep the last known good config if the source is unreachable.
**Avoid** runtime calls to the control plane.

analogy.title: A statically stable aircraft
analogy.story: When the pilot lets go of the controls, it naturally returns to level flight without anyone doing anything.
analogy.breaks: It costs idle capacity, so you're paying for resilience you hope not to use.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: An AZ loss becomes a non-event.

check.q: What does 'statically stable' mean for a system?
check.a: It keeps operating correctly through a dependency failure without needing any changes or new resources.

cascading-failures-and-the-danger-of-tig.core: Cascading failures spread when components are tightly coupled. One slow dependency exhausts callers' threads, retries amplify load and shared resources propagate the failure, turning a local fault into a global outage.

first_principles.problem: A slow recommendation service takes down checkout, login and search because everything waits on it synchronously.
derivation: **Decouple** with queues and asynchronous work; **degrade gracefully**.

analogy.title: Falling dominoes vs. firebreaks
analogy.story: Tightly packed dominoes all fall; gaps (firebreaks) stop the chain.

example.title: A retry storm
flow: B retries 3x, A retries 3x → 9x load on C
Fix: retry budget + breaker at B

check.q: How do layered retries cause cascading failure?
check.a: Each layer multiplies retries, flooding the struggling dependency with exponentially more load.

game-days-practicing-for-the-unthinkable.core: You prepare for black swans by practising failure. Game days deliberately simulate large-scale failures (region loss, control-plane outage, dependency blackout) in a controlled way, to test architecture, runbooks and people.

first_principles.problem: Teams read about static stability but never verify that their systems actually behave that way.
truths: Controlled failure is cheaper than real failure.

analogy.title: Military war games
analogy.story: Simulated battles reveal weaknesses in plans before real combat.
analogy.breaks: Start in staging, and production game days need careful blast-radius control.

example.title: A control-plane game day
flow: Hypothesis: traffic unaffected if EC2 APIs denied
Observe: autoscaler fails, but static capacity serves
Finding: deploy pipeline blocked → add fallback

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The weakness is found on a Tuesday, not during a real outage.

check.q: What should every game day define before starting?
check.a: A hypothesis about expected behaviour and abort criteria to stop if impact exceeds limits.
